A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same ViTaM-D work, and their pages, equations and displays are readable. However, v1 includes Appendices A–B, while v2 redirects their analyses and detailed flow architecture to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. Those portions cannot be fully matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original DexYCB and HOT reconstruction results, force-optimization experiments, and appendix analyses of flow prediction and point-pair selection.

after.justification: v2 reports reconstruction comparisons, contact-constraint ablations, force-optimization results, and an original real-world reconstruction example.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a contact constraint to the previously visual-only reconstruction stage. Contact states obtained from tactile sensors or a PointNet classifier constrain object SDF prediction, and Equation 8 expands the training objective from three losses to four. This changes the proposed procedure; the underlying DF-Field and subsequent hand-pose optimization remain.

E1.justification: DexYCB and the same 600-sequence, five-category HOT dataset are retained. Section 6.6 adds a limited real-world deformable-object scenario: a simulation-trained network reconstructing an unseen stuffed toy using actual tactile and depth measurements. 'Stuffed Animals' becoming 'Stuffed Toys' does not establish another HOT category.

E2.justification: v1 Table 1 compares against gSDF and HOTrack on DexYCB and reports only its own variants on HOT. v2 retains those comparators and adds Zhang et al. [40] on both datasets, ViTaM on HOT, and CPF and TOCH as alternative refinements on HOT. This substantially expands comparisons relevant to deformable reconstruction and contact refinement.

E3.justification: Section 6.5 changes the stated DexYCB fixed-force setting from 0.5 for every hand region to 0.5 for regions near objects at 3 mm; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. v2 also introduces contact-source controls and a simulation-trained real-world testing protocol. Shared dataset splits, metrics and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The reported analyses are substantially reorganized. Table 2 changes from testing direct tactile-feature fusion to comparing no contact constraint with ground-truth, tactile and PointNet-derived contact states; Section 6.6 adds a real-world transfer case study. v1's flow-accuracy, flow-module and keypoint-versus-all-vertices analyses are not reproduced in v2, which instead references unavailable supplementary material. Their retention or revision cannot be checked.

E5.justification: Both supplied PDFs report refinement time as 3.5 ± 0.5 seconds per frame and provide no repeated-run counts, seeds, accuracy confidence intervals or significance tests. v1's additional appendix timing entries use the same reporting practice; their absence does not establish a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds numerical results for the new comparators and contact ablations, plus real-world qualitative evidence. For example, HOT refinement results now include CPF at 11.9/7.8/37.5 and TOCH at 13.5/9.3/34.1 for MPJPE/PD/CIoU. Shared DexYCB scores and the final HOT optimization scores remain unchanged. HOT unrefined IoU changes from 80.5% to 81.0% alongside the method revision, so this is not an unchanged-method performance gain. v1's appendix result tables are unavailable in v2.

T1.justification: v2 formally introduces binary contact states and a contact-loss definition in Equation 7, incorporated into Equation 8. The original potential-energy, barrier-energy and hand-pose optimization formulations remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof is supplied; the main mathematical addition is the contact constraint.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain ViTaM-D, DF-Field and HOT. The abstract and introduction revise the reconstruction-stage claim to include contact constraints, and the abstract now explicitly claims superiority over previous hand-pose refinement methods. These extend the existing contribution claims without replacing the paper's central objective.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting improved reconstruction to contact constraints and directly measured contact information, including the usefulness of predicted contacts when tactile hardware is unavailable. It removes v1's explanation that gSDF's lower penetration depth results from incomplete object reconstruction. The general rationale for combining visual geometry with tactile contact information remains.

D1.justification: Reproducibility information changes substantially: v1's explicit flow-matching computation and feature widths are no longer included, with v2 referring readers to unavailable supplementary material. v2 adds farthest-point sampling, the contact threshold and loss weight, and identifies the ViTaM glove and Photoneo MotionCam M+ hardware. It also replaces a promised release with a project URL and a statement that code, models and datasets are available; actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds ViTaM, Incremental Potential Contact, Zhang et al.'s depth-based reconstruction and TOCH references. The introduction and related work explicitly distinguish ViTaM-D from ViTaM's direct visual-tactile fusion, and Section 3 attributes the barrier energy to Incremental Potential Contact. The broader research positioning and existing literature survey remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the method, dataset and experiment descriptions are rewritten or condensed. VDT-Net and FO terminology is largely replaced by descriptive stage names, detailed flow exposition becomes a supplementary reference, and the document adds a real-world section and acknowledgements. These constitute extensive editorial restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is rearranged into a first-page column, and the sensor-layout illustration is resized and moved earlier. The pipeline diagram adds the contact constraint, Table 1 expands the comparator rows, and Table 2 has a different structure and purpose. Figure 4 replaces HOT initial/final examples with comparator panels, while a new real-world Figure 6 replaces the previously supplied flow illustration. These are substantial display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: The new HOT baselines and CPF/TOCH controls provide stronger evidence for claims that v1 supported mainly through comparisons among its own variants; the real-world example also adds practical evidence. These benefits are tempered by the unavailable appendix analyses and reduced flow-architecture detail. The new contact loss also needs clarification: Equation 7 sums signed distances while claiming to enforce zero contact distance. The comparative evidence supports a limited net improvement despite these losses in auditability and clarity.
